lead: Powder metallurgy makes a metal part by pressing fine metal powder into a die shape and heating it below the melting point. The particles weld by diffusion, so the part needs little or no machining. The route suits small, complex parts in large numbers: gears, bushes, self-lubricating bearings, tungsten carbide inserts and magnets. It also handles metals that are hard to cast or machine, and mixtures that do not mix even in a melt, such as copper–graphite for brushes, copper–tungsten for contacts, or tungsten carbide with a cobalt binder. The price is porosity, which lowers strength and ductility.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for how particles deform plastically and lock together under pressure, and the casting unit for the contrast with solidification.

blocks.text: Powder making fixes particle size and shape. Water atomisation: high-pressure water jets break a molten metal stream into droplets that freeze irregular and spongy; cheap, used for iron and copper. Gas atomisation: inert gas makes round droplets; spherical powder flows well but costs more, used for superalloys and aluminium. Oxide reduction: a metal oxide is heated with carbon or hydrogen, leaving sponge metal; iron and tungsten powders come this way. Electrolysis: direct current deposits pure dendritic powder from a salt solution. Pulverising: crushing and ball milling break brittle metal or sponge into powder. Carbonyl process: a metal carbonyl vapour decomposes into very fine, pure, round powder.

Powder tests predict die filling. Particle size comes from sieving or microscopy; shape from a micrograph. Apparent density is loose powder mass divided by its volume. Tap density is measured after tapping the container, so it is higher. Flow rate is the time for 50 g to pass a standard funnel. Free-flowing round powder fills a die evenly.

Blending mixes powders and additives. A lubricant such as zinc stearate, about 0.5–1 % by mass, lowers die-wall friction. Graphite can do the same and add carbon. A poor mix gives density variation and weak spots.

Compaction presses the blended powder into a die with upper and lower punches. Pressure is roughly 100–800 MPa. Particles first slide and rearrange, then deform plastically and cold-weld at contacts. The compact is called green because it is unsintered. Green density ρg = m/V is its mass divided by its volume. Green strength is the bending or crushing strength before sintering; it must survive ejection and handling.
ρ<sub>g</sub> = m / V,   P = 1 − ρ<sub>g</sub>/ρ<sub>s</sub>,   T<sub>s</sub> = (0.7 to 0.9) T<sub>m</sub>
blocks.where: ρ<sub>g</sub> is green density (g/cm³); m is compact mass (g); V is compact volume (cm³); P is porosity as a fraction; ρ<sub>s</sub> is solid metal density (g/cm³); T<sub>s</sub> is sintering temperature (K), usually 0.7–0.9 T<sub>m</sub> and often about 0.7–0.8 T<sub>m</sub> for iron and copper base parts; T<sub>m</sub> is melting temperature (K).

blocks.text: Porosity P = 1 − ρ<sub>g</sub>/ρ<sub>s</sub>, where ρ<sub>s</sub> is the solid metal density. For iron ρ<sub>s</sub> = 7.87 g/cm³. A green density of 6.8 g/cm³ leaves P = 0.136, or 13.6 % pores. More pressure raises green density, but friction and trapped air limit it. Stepped parts need separate punches; undercuts cannot be pressed.

Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) fills a rubber bag with powder and presses it in a fluid. Pressure acts from all sides, so density is uniform and large parts are possible. Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) uses hot gas to close pores; it belongs with the high-pressure powder processes in Unit 7. Roll compaction feeds powder between rolls and makes a green strip. Metal injection moulding mixes fine powder with polymer binder, moulds a small complex shape, removes the binder, and sinters it.

Sintering heats the green part below its melting point, usually 0.7–0.9 T<sub>m</sub> (often about 0.7–0.8 T<sub>m</sub> for iron and copper base parts), where T<sub>m</sub> is the absolute melting temperature. Particles stay solid. Atoms diffuse, necks grow between touching particles, and pores shrink. Three stages: initial necking at contacts; intermediate stage with rounded pores and fast density rise; final stage with closed or isolated pores. The part densifies and gains strength.

Atmosphere protects the metal. Hydrogen reduces surface oxides. Nitrogen is a cheaper inert carrier. Endogas, made by burning a hydrocarbon with limited air, supplies CO, H<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>. A continuous belt furnace has a preheat zone, a hot sinter zone and a cooling zone. Batch vacuum furnaces suit reactive metals. Spark plasma sintering passes pulsed current through a graphite die and powder under pressure, so heating is fast and grain growth is limited; it is a specialised route.

Finishing corrects size and properties. Sizing presses the part in a die to fix dimensions. Coining presses it for sharper detail and higher density. Repressing and resintering repeat compaction and heating. Infiltration melts copper into an iron skeleton to fill pores. Impregnation fills pores with oil or resin; oil-filled bronze bushes are self-lubricating.

Density controls properties. Pores lower strength, ductility and impact resistance; hardness follows the metal matrix. Advantages: near-net shape, little machining, controlled porosity, mixed compositions. Limits: powder and die cost, shape limits, residual porosity. Uses include gears, bushes, oil-impregnated bearings, tungsten carbide inserts with cobalt binder, and powder magnets.

examples.question: An iron gear blank of volume 12.5 cm³ is die compacted to a green density of 6.8 g/cm³. Solid iron has density 7.87 g/cm³ and melts at 1538 °C. Find the powder mass, the green porosity, and a sintering temperature range using 0.7–0.8 T<sub>m</sub>. Give a common furnace value.
steps: Volume V = 12.5 cm³ and green density ρ<sub>g</sub> = 6.8 g/cm³.
Solid density ρ<sub>s</sub> = 7.87 g/cm³. Porosity P = 1 − 6.8/7.87 = 1 − 0.864 = 0.136.
A common furnace setting is 1120 °C in a hydrogen–nitrogen atmosphere.
examples.answer: The powder mass is 85 g, the green porosity is 0.136 (13.6 %), and sintering is at 1267.7–1448.8 K (994.7–1175.8 °C), commonly 1120 °C.

traps: Sintering does not melt the powder. The particles stay solid and bond by diffusion; liquid-phase sintering is a special case, not the standard P/M route.
Use green density to find the mass of a green compact, not solid density. Solid density would give the mass of a pore-free part.
Apparent density is loose powder density; tap density is after tapping; green density is the compacted part. Do not swap these terms.
Higher porosity lowers strength and ductility. It does not raise hardness; hardness mainly follows the metal matrix.
Zinc stearate is a die-wall lubricant, not a sintering aid and not the structural binder used in metal injection moulding.

quiz.q: Name two powder-making methods and two powder tests.
quiz.a: Water atomisation and oxide reduction are powder-making methods. Apparent density and flow rate are powder tests; particle size and tap density are also valid.

quiz.q: Why is sintering done below the melting point?
quiz.a: Below the melting point the particles remain solid, so the compact keeps its shape. Atoms diffuse across particle contacts, necks grow, and pores shrink, giving a bonded part without a liquid pool.

quiz.q: A compact has volume 10 cm³ and green density 6.5 g/cm³. Solid density is 7.87 g/cm³. Find the powder mass and green porosity.
Copper melts at 1085 °C. Give a sintering range at 0.7–0.8 T<sub>m</sub> in °C.
quiz.a: T<sub>m</sub> = 1085 + 273 = 1358 K. 0.7 T<sub>m</sub> = 950.6 K and 0.8 T<sub>m</sub> = 1086.4 K. In Celsius this is about 678–813 °C.

quiz.q: Why can an oil-impregnated bronze bush work as a self-lubricating bearing?
quiz.a: The sintered bush keeps interconnected porosity, and vacuum impregnation fills these pores with oil. During running the bush warms, the oil expands and seeps out of the interconnected pores to lubricate the shaft. When the bearing cools after stopping, capillary action draws the oil back into the pores. Too much porosity weakens the bush, so density is balanced against oil capacity.

quiz.q: Why is a simple die press poor for an undercut shape, and how does cold isostatic pressing help?
quiz.a: A die press ejects the part along one axis, so an undercut would catch on the die. Cold isostatic pressing uses fluid pressure on a rubber bag, pressing from all sides; a flexible bag can form shapes that cannot be ejected from a rigid die, and density is more uniform.

quiz.q: What does endogas do in a sintering furnace?
quiz.a: Endogas is a protective gas made by burning a hydrocarbon with limited air. It supplies CO, H<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>, which keep oxygen away and help reduce surface oxides so particle contacts can bond.

beyond: Not for the exam. Automotive powder metallurgy now makes connecting rods, synchroniser rings and sinter-hardened gears in millions. Metal injection moulding supplies small surgical and dental parts with complex shapes. Additive manufacturing uses gas-atomised spherical powder in powder-bed fusion, so powder testing methods carry over directly. Research looks at spark plasma sintering, high-entropy alloy powders and binder jetting. Search for sinter-hardening, metal injection moulding feedstock and powder-bed fusion powder reuse.
